question: What is the meaning of acidification potential (ap) in relation to material layers, materials?
description: The Acidification Potential (AP) in relation to material layers, materials, refers to the potential of a material to contribute to acid rain, which is a form of pollution that can have harmful effects on the environment, including water bodies, soil, and plant life. In the context of the provided text, AP is one of the three indicators used for the Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) of building materials, alongside the Global Warming Potential (GWP) and Primary Energy Intensity (PEI). These indicators help assess the environmental impact of materials during their manufacturing phase, considering factors such as emissions of acidic compounds that can lead to acidification of ecosystems. The AP value is expressed in [kgSO2/kg], indicating the amount of sulfur dioxide (SO2) emitted per kilogram of material produced. This assessment is crucial for evaluating the sustainability and environmental friendliness of building materials.

are used for the LCA, namely the Global Warming Potential (GWP), the 
Acidification Potential (AP) and Primary Energy Intensity (PEI), 
expressed in [kgCO2/kg], [kgSO2/kg] and [MJ/kg], respectively. For all 
three indicators, only the manufacturing phase is considered. By linking 
the mass of each material-layer of an element to the grades from 1 to 5, 
as well as to the indicators, the recycling potential and the environ­
mental impact of a building is assessed. 
For generating an MP, information about the material composition 
and geometry is required, which is obtained from the BIM-model. In 
detail, these are all material-layers of a building element (e.g. multi- 
layered wall with concrete, insulation and plaster) with their respec­
tive layer thicknesses and volumes. In order to obtain the mass of a 
material, the density and volume is required. The density is obtained 
from the IBO-database, whereas the volume of a material is obtained 
from the BIM-model. In our previous research, the generation of the 
BIM-based MP was conducted through a bi-directional connection of 
BIM with a material inventory and analysis tool, thus allowing a semi- 
automated workflow. As this is an effortful process, within this paper, 
the semi-automated workflow is not applied. Therefore, the required 
information from the BIM-model is obtained by exporting a spreadsheet 
and mapping the grades from 1 to 5 to the material layers. The main 
obstacle is the acquisition of the required information in order to enable 
the generation of an information rich BIM, since the information about 
the existing building is not sufficient. 
2.2. Adaptation of the MP-assessment method 
The planning documentation on existing buildings is seldom accu­
rate and represents a vague picture of buildings, as previous research has 
shown (Koutamanis et al., 2018; Bergsdal et al., 2007). Lack of infor­
mation represents a great challenge for the efficient compilation of an 
MP. Following information of the assessed building is required for the 
generation of an MP on component level (e.g. walls and slabs): all ma­
terial layers (name of material), thickness, dimensions of the compo­
nent, volume of each material layer (obtained from BIM) and 
separability of material layers. The MP-assessment method does not 
enable a direct integration of separation techniques, as it is based on 
downgrading of material grades. Accordingly, the separability is 
considered as follows: the recycling potential of materials, which are 
difficult to separate from the enclosed layer due to e.g. adhesives used 
for bonding, are downgraded, which means that in such a case a material 
with grade 3 is downgraded to grade 4. Materials which can be sepa­
rated with low effort and do not lead to contamination of the enclosed 
layers, are not downgraded (e.g. screws, nails, dowels). Within this 
paper, the MP-assessment method was applied on a real use case, where 
through destructive methods the separability of materials was analyzed 
on selected building elements as well as documented. As this research is 
based on real data acquired on site, as described in section 2.3, it delivers 
reliable information regarding the separability of materials. As the 
proposed MP-assessment method was initially developed for the build­
ing design stage, as described in 2.1, the quality of the materials did not 
play a crucial role. However, for existing buildings the quality has to be 
integrated in the assessment since at the end-of-life stage the quality of 
material might vary. Accordingly, within the adapted MP, the assigned 
grades from 1 to 5 are downgraded if a material has a lower quality at 
the end-of-life stage.
